field_notes.name: Charring a pepper
field_notes.body: The same dry cast-iron pan from July works — but peppers take longer and need to steam afterward. Char them on all sides until the skin is mostly blackened. Drop them into a bowl, cover tight, and leave them for 15 minutes. The skin will slip off cleanly. What's underneath is something the raw pepper never hinted at.

field_notes.name: Figs and time.
field_notes.body: A ripe fig goes from perfect to past-peak in about 24 hours. Buy them the day you plan to eat them, or the day before. If they're already splitting at the base, eat them today. This isn't a problem — it's the season telling you something.

field_notes.name: You don't need to salt eggplant.
field_notes.body: Salting was right for older varieties, which were genuinely bitter. Modern cultivars have had that bred out. What actually matters is high heat. A crowded pan steams; a hot, uncrowded pan chars. Give it room, leave it alone, and it becomes something worth eating.

field_notes.name: August at the fish counter.
field_notes.body: Yellowtail is still running. White sea bass is having its best weeks. Pacific swordfish shows up at some counters. The question from last month still applies: not 'Do you have salmon?' but 'What came in today?' In August, the honest answer is often better than what you planned.

local_ritual.label: San Diego ritual
local_ritual.name: Go to the market without a list.
local_ritual.description: August at a San Diego farmers market is worth giving yourself a slow hour. Walk the whole thing once before buying anything. Let what looks best decide the week.

one_thing_to_notice.headline: The color of a ripe fig.
one_thing_to_notice.body: A ripe fig darkens all the way to deep purple-black and sometimes splits at the base. Look for a small bead of sweetness near the stem. That's the one to buy.

guides.name: Adela

guides.voice: Warm, precise, and slightly impatient with under-ripe fruit.
guides.notices: Fragrance first. Color second. The shoulder near the stem of a nectarine.

quotes.nectarines: A nectarine that doesn't smell like anything won't improve on the counter. It just gets softer.
quotes.figs: You smell a fig before you taste it. That's how you know.

figs.name: Figs
figs.why_now: Mission figs peak in late July through August. The window is short — often just two or three weeks of genuinely perfect fruit. What you find now was picked ripe and won't be available like this again until next year.
how_to_choose: Deep purple to almost black — that's ripe, not overripe
Slightly soft when gently pressed, especially near the base
Sometimes splitting at the base — that's a good sign
A small bead of sweetness near the stem means it's ready
Avoid pale green or tan figs; they haven't ripened
figs.buy_this_much: 1 pint for the week. Plan to eat most of them within two days of buying.
figs.price_note: Figs are briefly abundant in August and reasonably priced at farmers markets. Grocery store figs are available but often picked underripe for transport — the farmers market version is worth the detour this month.

figs.weekend_use: The weekend plate: halved figs, torn burrata, prosciutto, arugula, olive oil, and flaky salt. Eat with bread.
figs.storage: Counter for a day, two at most. Refrigerate only if necessary and use immediately after. Do not buy them expecting them to keep.
figs.one_thing_to_learn: A fig ripens from the outside in, not the inside out. The color tells you something. Black-purple with a soft give near the base is ready. A hard, pale fig won't ripen meaningfully on the counter — it will soften but not sweeten the way a tree-ripened one does.

bell-peppers.name: Bell peppers
bell-peppers.tile_uses: Rice bowls, tacos, house flavor, chicken
bell-peppers.why_now: Red and yellow bell peppers are fully ripened green peppers — and August is when they arrive in abundance. The color change takes weeks on the plant, which is why they cost more and why they taste completely different. The bitterness is gone. What's left is sweet, thick, and worth roasting.
how_to_choose: Fully red or fully yellow — no green patches
Firm and heavy for their size
Glossy skin without soft spots
The thicker the walls, the better for roasting
bell-peppers.buy_this_much: 3–4 peppers for the week. Two go into the house flavor; the rest go into meals.
bell-peppers.price_note: Red and yellow peppers cost more than green because they've spent longer on the plant. In August, supply increases and prices tend to soften slightly.

flavor_paths.name: Charred
flavor_paths.description: The house flavor. Blistered in a dry pan, steamed, peeled, blended with garlic, oil, and sherry vinegar.

flavor_paths.name: Raw
flavor_paths.description: Sliced thin in a taco or rice bowl. The sweetness holds without cooking.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted whole
flavor_paths.description: In the oven at high heat. Collapse into softness, serve alongside chicken or fold into pasta.

weekday_uses: Sliced raw into tacos or rice bowls
Roasted and added to a rice bowl or pasta
Used as the base for the charred pepper sauce
bell-peppers.weekend_use: Roasted whole alongside chicken thighs. Tear them open over the plate.
bell-peppers.storage: Refrigerator crisper. Up to a week before roasting; a few days once roasted.
bell-peppers.one_thing_to_learn: A fully red bell pepper and a green bell pepper are the same vegetable at different points of ripeness. The green one was picked early. Weeks more on the plant produce the color, the sweetness, and the complete absence of that grassy bitterness. This is also why charring works so well on red peppers — there's actual sugar to caramelize.
bell-peppers.market_question: Are these fully ripened on the plant, or ripened in transit?

eggplant.name: Eggplant
eggplant.tile_uses: House flavor base, rice bowls, pasta, sides
eggplant.why_now: Eggplant peaks in late summer — August is when Southern California farms produce them in abundance. The flesh is less bitter than in off-season months, and the skin is thinner. What arrives now roasts into something deeply savory with minimal effort.
how_to_choose: Firm with no soft spots — a soft eggplant will be bitter and seedy
Glossy, taut skin rather than dull or wrinkled
Lighter weight for its size often means fewer seeds
The cap and stem should still look fresh, not dry
eggplant.buy_this_much: 1 large eggplant or 2 small ones for the week.
eggplant.price_note: Eggplant is inexpensive in August when supply peaks. Italian eggplant (the long, narrow variety) and Japanese eggplant roast particularly well.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted high and hot
flavor_paths.description: Cut into chunks, high heat, left alone. It collapses into something sweet and savory.

flavor_paths.name: Charred whole
flavor_paths.description: Over an open flame or under a broiler until the skin is completely black. Scoop out the smoky flesh.

flavor_paths.name: Pan-fried
flavor_paths.description: Sliced thick, olive oil, high heat. Leave it alone until it releases from the pan.

weekday_uses: Roasted in chunks and added to a rice bowl
Pan-fried thick slices alongside chicken or fish
Folded into pasta with cherry tomatoes and basil
eggplant.weekend_use: Charred whole over flame or under the broiler, flesh scooped out and mixed with olive oil, garlic, and lemon. Serve with bread.
eggplant.storage: Counter for a day or two, then refrigerator. Don't buy it more than three or four days before you plan to use it.
eggplant.one_thing_to_learn: You don't need to salt modern eggplant. The salting-and-draining method was developed for older, bitter varieties. Current cultivars have had the bitterness bred out. What actually matters is heat — a crowded pan steams and makes it soggy. Give the pieces room, use a hot pan, and leave them alone until they release and color.
eggplant.market_question: What variety is this? Italian or Japanese?

cherry-tomatoes.name: Cherry tomatoes
cherry-tomatoes.why_now: Cherry tomatoes are still running strong in August and can be exceptional — concentrated flavor, thin skins that burst easily. Where July favored big heirlooms for slicing and eating raw, August is when cherry tomatoes hit their stride, especially the sungold and mixed varieties.
how_to_choose: Firm but not hard — should give slightly when pressed
Deep, even color throughout (red, orange, or yellow depending on variety)
Fragrant at the stem end
Avoid any with wrinkled skins or soft spots
cherry-tomatoes.buy_this_much: 1 pint for the week — they'll appear in pasta, tacos, and rice bowls, and disappear faster than expected.
cherry-tomatoes.price_note: Cherry tomatoes are widely available in August at most grocery stores and farmers markets. Mixed varieties at farmers markets often include sungolds and grape tomatoes, which are worth seeking out.

flavor_paths.name: Burst in oil
flavor_paths.description: In a hot pan with olive oil until they split. The pasta sauce that doesn't need a jar.

flavor_paths.name: Raw
flavor_paths.description: Halved in a taco or rice bowl. Their acidity does the seasoning.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted
flavor_paths.description: In the oven at high heat until collapsed and slightly caramelized. Different from burst — sweeter, more concentrated.

weekday_uses: Burst in olive oil and tossed with pasta
Halved raw in tacos or rice bowls
Eaten as a snack, straight from the container
cherry-tomatoes.weekend_use: Roasted slowly at lower heat until they collapse and concentrate. Spoon over burrata or add to a grain salad.
cherry-tomatoes.storage: Counter at room temperature, away from direct sunlight. Do not refrigerate — cold ruins the texture and flavor. Use within three or four days.
cherry-tomatoes.one_thing_to_learn: Bursting cherry tomatoes in a hot pan is one of the most reliable weekday techniques. The key is patience — add them to a hot pan with olive oil, don't stir, and let them blister and split on their own. The skin will tighten, then burst, releasing liquid that becomes the sauce. Stir once they've started to collapse. Add garlic and basil after the heat is off.
cherry-tomatoes.market_question: Do you have sungolds? What's the sweetest variety this week?

jalapenos.name: Jalapeños
jalapenos.why_now: Jalapeños are peak summer, and in August the heat and color variation is at its widest. Green jalapeños are grassier; red jalapeños (fully ripened) are fruitier and a little hotter. The house flavor this month uses them alongside peppers — but they earn their place in almost every savory dish on the table.
how_to_choose: Firm and glossy, no soft spots
Green is grassy and mild-to-medium; red is fruity and a bit hotter
Streaks of tan or brown on the skin (corking) indicate more heat — a sign of stress on the plant, which concentrates the capsaicin
Smaller jalapeños tend to be hotter than larger ones
jalapenos.buy_this_much: 3–4 jalapeños. Two go into the house flavor; the rest carry the week.
jalapenos.price_note: Jalapeños are inexpensive year-round but at their best now. Look for them at Mexican grocery stores or the farmers market for the freshest selection.

flavor_paths.name: Charred into the sauce
flavor_paths.description: The house flavor: charred alongside red peppers, blended smooth.

flavor_paths.name: Raw, sliced thin
flavor_paths.description: In tacos, rice bowls, or the drink. The raw crunch is different from the cooked version.

flavor_paths.name: Quick-pickled
flavor_paths.description: Sliced into rings with vinegar, sugar, and salt. Ready in an hour, good for a week.

weekday_uses: Sliced thin into tacos or rice bowls
A few rounds dropped into the drink
Diced and stirred into scrambled eggs
jalapenos.weekend_use: Quick-pickled jalapeño rings. Slice thin, cover with equal parts white vinegar and water, a pinch of sugar and salt, a garlic clove. Ready in an hour. Good on almost everything for the rest of the week.
jalapenos.storage: Refrigerator crisper, up to two weeks. They dry out on the counter.
jalapenos.one_thing_to_learn: Heat level in jalapeños varies seed to seed and plant to plant — you can't know from appearance alone. Taste a small piece before adding them to a dish. The seeds and membranes hold most of the heat; removing them makes the pepper significantly milder while keeping the flavor.
jalapenos.market_question: Are these mild or hot this week?

zucchini.name: Zucchini
zucchini.why_now: Zucchini is abundantly available through August and at its best when small to medium sized — the larger ones that appear later in the season can be watery. Right now they're quick to cook, mild enough to take on other flavors, and cheap enough to use without planning precisely.
how_to_choose: Small to medium — 6 to 8 inches is ideal; larger ones are often seedy and watery
Firm with no soft spots
Glossy skin, no bruising
The ends should look fresh, not dry or shriveled
zucchini.buy_this_much: 3–4 medium zucchini. They cook down significantly, so buy more than you think you need.
zucchini.price_note: Zucchini is very inexpensive in August — often one of the lowest-cost items in the basket. Any grocery store will have them.

zucchini.weekend_use: Shaved raw into thin ribbons, dressed simply with olive oil, lemon, and flaky salt. Serve alongside grilled chicken or fish.
zucchini.storage: Refrigerator crisper, up to a week. Don't wash before storing.
zucchini.one_thing_to_learn: Zucchini releases a lot of water. To avoid a soggy pan, don't crowd them — cook in a single layer with space between pieces, and don't stir too often. High heat and patience are the technique. Once the water has cooked off, what's left will actually brown.
zucchini.market_question: Do you have any smaller zucchini? Or yellow squash?

basil.name: Basil
basil.why_now: Basil is at peak abundance in August — warm nights and hot days produce the most fragrant leaves of the year. If you kept a potted plant from July, it's probably thriving. This is the month to use it generously.
how_to_choose: Bright, vivid green — yellow or black-edged leaves are past their best
Fragrant when you brush the leaves
Stems still firm and upright
Avoid bunches stored in cold refrigerator display — cold turns basil black
basil.buy_this_much: 1 large bunch, or one potted plant (which lasts longer and regrows if you harvest the tops).
basil.price_note: Basil is widely available and inexpensive in August. A potted plant from a grocery store costs about the same as a bunch and will yield multiple harvests.

weekday_uses: Torn over pasta at the end, after the heat is off

basil.weekend_use: A rough basil oil: blend a handful of leaves with olive oil, a garlic clove, and salt. Spoon over burrata, chicken, or fish.
basil.storage: Keep at room temperature in a glass of water like flowers — never in the refrigerator. Cut the stems every few days. Lasts up to a week this way.
basil.one_thing_to_learn: Basil blackens from the cold, not from age. Refrigerator storage turns it black overnight. Keep it on the counter in water, and it will outlast basil stored in the fridge by several days. The fragrance concentrates if you let it sit somewhere warm.
basil.market_question: Is this Italian basil or Thai basil? Do you have lemon basil?

nectarines.name: Nectarines
nectarines.why_now: Nectarines are peaches without the fuzz, and in August they often hit their stride when peach season begins to wind down. The flavor is similar — sweet, aromatic, deeply summery — but the skin is thinner and doesn't need peeling. This is the last good stone fruit window before fall.
how_to_choose: Fragrant at the stem end — this is the most reliable test
Gives slightly when gently pressed near the top
Deep color, though variety affects this (yellow and white varieties both have peak moments)
Avoid hard nectarines — they were picked underripe and won't improve meaningfully
nectarines.buy_this_much: 4–5 nectarines for the week. They don't all need to be eaten at once.
nectarines.price_note: Stone fruit is still affordable in August, though supply begins to thin by late in the month. Buy them when you see good ones — the window doesn't come back.

flavor_paths.name: Nearly nothing
flavor_paths.description: Sliced and eaten as they are. A pinch of flaky salt if you want to push it.

flavor_paths.name: With yogurt
flavor_paths.description: Sliced on Greek yogurt in the morning, maybe a little honey. That's it.

flavor_paths.name: On the plate
flavor_paths.description: Alongside burrata when figs aren't enough or aren't available.

weekday_uses: Sliced on Greek yogurt in the morning

nectarines.weekend_use: Alongside the fig and burrata plate — or in place of figs if they weren't available. The combination of ripe stone fruit, good cheese, and cured meat holds up in either direction.
nectarines.storage: Counter until ripe. Eat within a day or two of peak ripeness. Do not refrigerate until fully ripe, and use quickly after.
nectarines.one_thing_to_learn: Nectarines and peaches are genetically almost identical — the difference is a single gene that determines whether the skin is fuzzy or smooth. Their flavor profiles and peak windows are nearly the same. If you're buying from a farmers market, ask which variety the grower would eat today. They usually know exactly which ones are ready.
